name: Paper & pulp
summary: Close your water loops further without salt build-up, and turn treated effluent into water you can use again.
title: Water reuse for paper and pulp mills
lede: Mills are being pushed to use less fresh water. The barrier to closing loops further is salt: chlorides, sulphates and calcium build up until they cause scaling, corrosion and quality problems. Danu Water removes them, so the water can keep circulating.
problem_intro: Paper is one of the most water-intensive industries, and many mills sit in regions where water is getting scarcer and discharge limits are tightening.
pains: Salt build-up in closed loops
Every time water is recirculated, dissolved salts concentrate. Above a threshold they cause deposits, scaling, corrosion and runnability problems.
Rising freshwater and discharge costs
Abstraction licences, water tariffs and effluent charges are all moving in one direction.
Water stress
In drought-prone regions, water restrictions can force mills to cut production.
Variable water
Mill water changes with grade, furnish and season. Fixed treatment systems struggle to keep up.
facts: Industrial pilot unit operating at WEPA's Bridgend mill, Wales, since October 2026
Seven-week pilot programme at Essity's Valls site, Spain, from November 2026
Letters of intent from WEPA and Essity

offerings.name: Recycle loop salt control
offerings.status_note: Industrial pilot at WEPA Bridgend; testing at Essity Valls from November 2026
offerings.what: A side-stream on the white water or process water loop that removes dissolved salts continuously, so the loop stays below the level where problems start.
benefits: Close loops further and cut freshwater intake
Less scaling, corrosion and deposit-related downtime
Steadier water chemistry for the paper machine
offerings.fit: Mills running tight water circuits, or planning to, where conductivity or hardness is the limit.

flow.clean: Low-salt water back to the loop
flow.caption: Danu Water takes a bleed from the white water loop, removes salts and returns low-salt water to stock preparation, so less fresh water is needed.

offerings.name: Treated effluent to fresh water
offerings.status_note: Freshwater stream tests in the Essity Valls programme
offerings.what: Polishing of biologically treated effluent to a quality that can replace part of the mill's freshwater intake, instead of sending it to discharge.
benefits: A water source the mill controls, independent of drought restrictions
Smaller discharge volumes and lower effluent charges
A step towards near-closed water use
offerings.fit: Mills with an effluent treatment plant and a freshwater supply that is costly, constrained or under pressure.

flow.caption: After the mill's existing effluent treatment, Danu Water removes dissolved salts so the water can go back into the mill rather than to the river.

offerings.name: Concentrate as a resource
offerings.what: Our process produces a small, concentrated salt stream rather than a dilute waste. We are working on routes to use it, rather than dispose of it.
benefits: Lower disposal volumes
Potential inputs for other industries, such as construction materials or fertiliser
offerings.fit: Sites where brine disposal is a cost or a permitting issue.

name: Mining & mine water
summary: Treat mine water for reuse instead of discharge, and manage salt in bioleaching circuits while keeping the metals.
title: Mine water and metals recovery
lede: Mine water is variable, often full of solids and dominated by different salts from one site to the next. Those are the conditions where conventional membranes struggle and where an adaptive system is useful.
problem_intro: Active and closed mines pump vast volumes of water that must be treated before release. At the same time, metal recovery processes like bioleaching are limited by salt they cannot easily remove.
pains: Treat-and-discharge costs
Large pumped volumes, treated in perpetuity at closed sites, with nothing recovered.
Every site is different
Some waters are chloride-dominated, others sulphate-dominated from pyrite oxidation. One fixed design does not fit all.
Solids and scaling
Reverse osmosis is easily fouled by solids and scaling minerals, which mine water carries in quantity.
Salt in leach circuits
In bioleaching, salt builds up in the recirculating solution and has to be controlled without losing copper or iron.
facts: Water-chemistry modelling across chloride-dominated, sulphate-dominated and mixed mine waters
Best suited to waters up to about 10,000 µS/cm, with a sweet spot below 5,000 µS/cm
In discussion with a copper bioleaching company on salt control

offerings.name: Mine water for reuse
offerings.status_note: Modelling across site types, including lime and caustic pre-treatment
offerings.what: Treatment of pumped mine water, after conventional settlement, to a quality that can be used for agriculture or industry rather than simply discharged.
benefits: Turns a perpetual treatment cost into a water resource
Tolerates the variability between and within sites
Handles conditions that foul reverse osmosis
offerings.fit: Mine water schemes with moderate salinity, particularly sulphate-dominated and mixed waters.

flow.caption: Danu Water sits after existing dosing and settlement, taking out the dissolved salts that stop mine water being reused.

offerings.name: Salt control in bioleaching
offerings.status_note: Technical discussions with an industry partner
offerings.what: Selective removal of sodium chloride from bioleach solutions, keeping copper and iron in the circuit so the iron can be reused by the bacteria.
benefits: Keeps salinity where the process needs it
Retains valuable copper and reusable iron
Reduces bleed and make-up volumes
offerings.fit: Heap and tank bioleaching of low and medium-grade copper ores, such as chalcopyrite.

flow.caption: Danu Water treats a bleed of the raffinate, removing sodium chloride and sending the solution, with its iron, back to the heap.

name: Distilling
summary: Get more from vinasse (dunder): water you can reuse and a potassium-rich concentrate, especially where water is scarce.
title: Water and vinasse in distilling
lede: For every litre of rum, a distillery produces many litres of vinasse, known as dunder in the Caribbean. It is strong, salty and hard to treat, and many distilleries are on islands where fresh water is precious.
problem_intro: We are looking at how Danu Water can help across the rum-making process, with a particular focus on Caribbean distilleries.
pains: Vinasse disposal
High-strength, high-salt and produced in large volumes, vinasse is difficult and costly to treat or discharge.
Limits on recycling dunder
Many distilleries already return some dunder to fermentation. Salt build-up limits how much they can reuse.
Scarce fresh water
Island distilleries depend on limited supplies for fermentation and cooling.
Lost nutrients
Vinasse is rich in potassium, a valuable fertiliser that is usually wasted.
facts: Early-stage work focused on Caribbean rum distilleries
Interested in speaking to distilleries willing to share water and vinasse data

offerings.name: Vinasse desalting and potassium recovery
offerings.what: Removal of salts from vinasse, producing a lower-salt stream that is easier to treat or recycle, and a potassium-rich concentrate.
benefits: More dunder can go back to fermentation
A fertiliser product instead of a disposal problem
Smaller, easier-to-treat effluent
offerings.fit: Molasses-based distilleries with vinasse disposal costs or a local need for fertiliser.

flow.caption: Danu Water treats vinasse after distillation, so more of it can be recycled and the salts become a potassium-rich product.

offerings.name: Process and cooling water reuse
offerings.what: Recovery of reusable water from distillery wastewater and cooling systems, reducing demand on scarce local supplies.
benefits: Lower freshwater use
Less exposure to supply restrictions
Reduced discharge

name: Municipal & utilities
summary: Turn treated municipal effluent into cooling water, so industry and data centres stop drawing on drinking water.
title: Effluent reuse for utilities and cooling
lede: Cooling is one of the largest uses of water in industry, and demand from data centres is rising fast. Much of it is still met with drinking-quality water. Treated municipal effluent is a reliable alternative, once the salts are dealt with.
problem_intro: Utilities are under pressure to free up supply capacity, while industrial and digital users need large, dependable volumes of cooling water.
pains: Competition for potable water
Every cubic metre of drinking water used for cooling is unavailable for homes and new development.
Salts limit cooling cycles
Hardness and dissolved salts cause scaling and corrosion, forcing frequent blowdown.
Effluent is underused
Treated effluent is a steady, local supply that is usually discharged.
By-products need a home
Treatment trains produce sludges and concentrates. Finding uses for them matters as much as the clean water.
facts: Concept design for a staged treatment train from municipal effluent to cooling water make-up
Initial market focus on the United States, designed with UK and EU regulations in mind
Conversations with data centre and water utility contacts in the US and Japan

offerings.name: Municipal effluent to cooling water
offerings.what: A treatment train that takes treated municipal effluent and produces cooling water make-up, with Danu Water removing the salts that limit reuse.
benefits: Frees potable supply for homes and growth
More cycles of concentration and less blowdown
By-products such as lime sludge can go to local farms as agricultural lime
offerings.fit: Utilities with industrial or power customers nearby, and users with large cooling demands.

flow.caption: Effluent from the treatment works is pre-treated, then Danu Water removes dissolved salts to meet cooling water quality.

offerings.name: Cooling water for data centres
offerings.what: Supplying data centres, including smaller edge sites, with cooling water made from effluent or lower-quality local water instead of mains supply.
benefits: Reduces the water footprint of computing
Eases local opposition and permitting
A route to water-as-a-service supply
offerings.fit: Operators and utilities planning data centre capacity in water-stressed areas.

offerings.name: Brackish and saline water
offerings.what: Treatment of wells and other water sources with rising salinity, where reverse osmosis struggles with solids, scaling or recovery.
benefits: High water recovery
A concentrate stream that can be used rather than dumped
offerings.fit: Communities and businesses whose water source is becoming saltier.
